notes:
Most of what I found is older commentary. The sources don't show any real split between Protestant traditions on this psalm. The only clear disagreements are over whether the psalm speaks directly of Christ, and over what verse 4 says about death. I found no Lutheran, Orthodox or prosperity/word-of-faith material on this chapter. The church labels in brackets are my own additions, not taken from the pages.

**Introduction**
- Ellicott (Anglican) calls it a hymn for worship, the first of five "Hallelujah" psalms. It was evidently composed for a time of great national depression, when the community, sick of dependence on the favour of foreign princes, turned more and more to the thought of the eternal righteousness and faithfulness of Jehovah. He links it to the Maccabean period (2nd century BC) because 1 Maccabees 2:63 seems to echo verse 4. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-146.html
- Gill (Baptist) mentions Jewish teachers who read it as about the exiles' return and the Messiah's time. He goes further: it is most true, that the psalm is concerning the Messiah and his kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-146.html
- Guzik/Boice (Enduring Word): this opens the five final psalms, where everything is praise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-146/

**v. 1**
- Guzik: "Hallelujah" joins *hallel* ("praise!") and *jah* (short for God's name). The psalmist praises himself and calls others to praise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-146/
- Spurgeon: the leader must stir up his own soul, not only urge others. Saying "Praise ye" without "Praise, O my soul" is a bad thing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/146-1.htm
- Gill: it is the heart God asks for, worship "in spirit and in truth." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-146.html
- Bible.org (Utley): "soul" (*nephesh*) means the whole person. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-146
- Catholic view (Augustine): the higher, reasoning part of the soul calls the troubled lower part back from worldly distraction to God. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801146.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik: compare Psalm 104:33. Clarke reads "while I have my being" as reaching into eternal existence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-146/
- Gill agrees: the praise continues after death, in the world to come. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-146.html
- Other readers take it as lifelong faithfulness, like "faithful unto death." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/psalms-146.html
- Augustine: since being and praise will both be everlasting, this "as long as" is truly long. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801146.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik: God is to be praised, but man is to be questioned. Even princes don't deserve our confidence. Kidner's modern equivalent of "princes" is "the influential." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-146/
- Pulpit Commentary: Israel kept leaning on Egypt, Assyria or its own leaders. After the exile, too much was expected of Zerubbabel. Cambridge thinks foreign rulers are meant, perhaps with a party pushing for an alliance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/146-3.htm
- Ellicott: the problem is princes' frailty as mortals, not their moodiness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-146.html
- "Help" can be translated "salvation." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/146-3.htm
- **Difference: does "son of man" point to Christ?** Gill says one Son of man, Jesus, may be trusted, because he is God as well as man. Barnes (Presbyterian) says The language here, however, it is scarcely necessary to say, does not refer to him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/146-3.htm
- Augustine: people cheer when a powerful man is promised as their rescuer, yet lose heart when told God will free them. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801146.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik/Boice: a wordplay. *Adam* (man) sounds like *adamah* (ground), so dirt returns to dirt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-146/
- Ellicott: echoes Genesis 2:7 and 3:19. The word "thoughts" appears only here, and its root sense is "fabrications." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-146.html
- Pulpit: his schemes are "nipped in the bud." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/146-4.htm
- Wesley (Methodist): "thoughts" means all his plans, for himself or for others. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/146.htm
- **Difference: what happens at death.** Some people read the last line as meaning the dead are not conscious. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/psalms-146.html
  - Gill answers that the soul is immortal and keeps thinking after death (citing Revelation 6:9). Only a man's plans end. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/146-4.htm
  - In Spurgeon's collection, Williamson says the spirit "goeth forth" and does not perish. Another writer notes the grammar: the spirit goes out, but "he" (the mortal part) returns to earth. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps146.cfm
  - Utley: the body returns to dust and the spirit, or life force, goes to Sheol. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-146
- Augustine: where is the pride now? The boaster's passing is a bad one. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801146.htm

**v. 5**
- Guzik: princes fail, but God never lets down those who hope in him. Spurgeon: quiet trust is among the sweetest music to God, and trusting man robs God of glory. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-146/
- Barnes: "Jacob" may mean the patriarch, or the whole nation, as opposed to pagan gods. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-146.html
- Ellicott: the word for "hope" is rare and means eager waiting. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-146.html
- Gill reads "the God of Jacob" as Christ, the Angel who wrestled with Jacob. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-146.html
- Augustine: God turned Jacob into Israel, "seeing God," and does the same for those he helps. He also reads "the Lord his God" through 1 Corinthians 8:6. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801146.htm

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: "truth" means faithfulness. Creation itself was a promise to the universe, as the covenant was to Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-146.html
- Keil-Delitzsch: men may want to help but can't, and they change their minds. God is almighty and keeps his promises. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/146-6.htm
- Trapp (via Guzik): God's "forever" is set against the mortal princes of verse 4. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-146/
- Gill again says the Maker here is Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/146-6.htm
- Augustine: the God who made everything "and all that is in them" made you, and cares even for sparrows and worms. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801146.htm

**v. 7**
- Spurgeon (via Guzik): a triple blessing: justice, bread, and liberty. Maclaren: every kind of hunger is a door for God to enter. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-146/
- A writer in Spurgeon's collection: God sometimes lets his people go hungry so he can help them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps146.cfm
- Utley: "prisoners" may also mean people trapped by sin or guilt. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-146-always-praising-always-trusting-always-blessed
- Gill takes it partly literally (manna, Jesus feeding the crowds) and partly spiritually (freedom from sin and Satan). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-146.html

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: blindness here most likely means distress and helplessness, not lack of spiritual insight. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-146.html
- Barnes: it could be bodily or mental blindness. The Geneva notes (Reformed): even when God afflicts the righteous, his fatherly love never fails. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/146-8.htm
- Maclaren (via Guzik): meant literally, but hinting at spiritual blindness too. Guzik matches each line to what Jesus did and concludes Jesus is the LORD. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-146/

**v. 9**
- Cambridge: foreigners, orphans and widows are the standard examples of people without protection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/146-9.htm
- Ellicott: "relieveth" is better "restoreth," perhaps picturing God as a witness in court. "Turneth upside down" means bending the path aside so it becomes crooked. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-146.html
- Spurgeon: everything goes wrong with the one who goes wrong. Le Blanc: Jacob himself was a stranger when God became his God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps146.cfm
- Maclaren (via Guzik): a true portrait of God needs this shadow. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-146/

**v. 10**
- Clarke (via Guzik): he reigns forever, so he can never fail Zion. Spurgeon: the psalm ends, but the praise does not. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-146/
- Utley: this is about the sovereignty of Israel's God. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-146

**Modern scholarship (NET Bible notes)**
- vv. 7–9: God is pictured as the just king, like ancient Near Eastern kings who were expected to protect foreigners, orphans and widows.
- v. 9: "twisted way" means the wicked suffer the results of their own actions.
- v. 8: "bowed down" may mean "discouraged."
- https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=psa+146
- Utley notes that two modern English versions (NEB and REB) re-read "forever" at the end of v. 6 as "the oppressed." https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-146
